 What to Know About Skyler Johnson, the Newly-Elected Board of Trustees Graduate Student Representative
 By
 Maya Johansen 
 Nov 10, 2026 5:59 pm 
 · Updated Nov 10, 2026 5:59 pm 
 Reading time: about 4 minutes
 Skyler Johnson J.D. ’28 was elected to be the Cornell Board of Trustees graduate and professional students representative on Oct. 1 after a campaign which focused on investing more in graduate programs, protecting against funding cuts and improving loans available to students. 
 In his election, Johnson beat out Rachel Davis, a second year Ph.D. student, and Kimberly McMillan M.B.A. ’28 to secure a two-year term as a student-elected trustee.  
 Pushing back against federal funding cuts and pushing for an overall increase in support for graduate student programs was a key part of Johnson’s focus. 
 “The University needs to continue to fight cuts and support graduate programs,” Johnson told The Sun. “It’s a big part of what makes Cornell University the elite institution that it is.” 
 Graduate programs have been affected by federal cuts to research and stop-work orders under the Trump administration. In 2025, Cornell saw over $250 million in research funding frozen and over 120 stop-work orders. Though the funding has since been restored with a federal settlement, researchers pointed to its impact on graduate students’ job security. 
 “I really focused on my campaign on … making sure that we can continue to keep open access to funding for students as we’ve seen federal cuts and as we’ve seen federal access to funding start to shudder,” Johnson said. 
 In addition, Johnson proposes that the University should expand or adapt its existing student loan programs to serve graduate students. 
 Federal loans for many graduate students were restricted under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed by President Donald Trump in August 2025. After July 1, 2026, graduate students can no longer take out Grad PLUS federal loans , and the parent version of the loan is severely capped and faces repayment restrictions. 
 University-funded loan programs are available only to undergraduates who demonstrate financial need, limiting graduate students to either federal loans, which face restrictions, or private loans. 
 Ideally, “the University could offer [graduate] students more favorable borrowing terms than they might otherwise receive through private lenders,” Johnson wrote in a statement to The Sun. 
 Johnson’s campaign also touched on expanding free access to the TCAT buses for graduate students. 
 After the first year of studies, undergraduate and graduate students both must pay for the TCAT, and are only exempt on weekends or after 6 p.m. on weekdays. Ph.D. candidates, graduate assistants and members of Cornell Graduate Students United , however, are exempt from paying for the TCAT for the duration of their studies. 
 “I would like to see [the fare exemption program] expanded to cover everyone in graduate and professional programs because of the economic strain that often falls on the student population,” he said. 
 Johnson told The Sun that TCAT access is one of his core issues because he believes it is an achievable goal that would have a tangible effect on students’ lives. 
 Johnson has extensive experience working in advocacy ranging from being a board member on Planned Parenthood Hudson Peconic Action Fund , being a board member of the Temple Beth Emeth Synagogue , to his position as the Cornell Law Student Association Vice President .  In addition, he is also the Co-President of OutLaw , Cornell Law’s LGBTQ organization. 
 “I think that those experiences overall have taught me how to have a voice, even in a room where people may disagree with me and in a room where I’m one of the most, if not the most, junior person,” Johnson said. “Being on a board like this where you become a colleague with executives and very accomplished individuals, you need to not be afraid to use your voice. Otherwise, you’ll very easily get drowned out.” 
 The Board of Trustees is vested with “supreme control” over the University, including all of its colleges and other units, according to their website. 
 As the graduate student representative , Johnson will serve as a full voting member for two years on the Board of Trustees. In addition, Johnson sits on committees including the Committee on Student Life to discuss issues directly related to campus life. 
 When asked about what success would look like for his tenure as the graduate student representative on the Board of Trustees, Johnson reiterated that he simply wants to “get the ball rolling” on his initiatives. 
 “Sucesss for me would be walking away knowing that I left the University a little better than I found it,” Johnson said.
 Maya Johansen Maya Johansen is a member of the Class of 2029 in the College of Arts and Sciences. She is a contributor for the news department and can be reached at mhj49@cornell.edu.
